correctness.rationale: For the inradius-one regular \(4n\)-gon, \(\|z\|_N\le\|z\|_2\le R\|z\|_N\) with \(R=\sec(\pi/(4n))\). The coefficient matrix of the Euler--Lagrange transform is Euclidean orthogonal up to \(\sqrt{\lambda^2+\mu^2}\), so the numerator is at most \(R^2\) times the defining denominator. At the balanced ratio, adjacent vertices symmetric about a facet normal send sum and difference to perpendicular facet-normal rays. At \(\mu/\lambda=\tan((2k+1)\pi/(4n))\), a quarter-turn vertex pair sends both transformed vectors to facet-normal rays of Euclidean length \(R\). Thus both the upper bound and the stated equality cases are exact.
risks: The theorem does not classify every equality ratio; no necessity statement is made.
The computational checks are supplementary only; the all-\(n\) statement rests on the symbolic proof.

Targeted full-text searches found no polygon, octagon, or dodecagon treatment. Public research-index searches covered the invariant name, regular-polygon aliases, the secant value, dodecagonal specialization, and the tangent resonance parameterization. value.rationale: The source introduces \(L_{\mathrm{YJ}}\) as a two-parameter measure of departure from Hilbert geometry. The theorem identifies a sharp Euclidean-distortion ceiling on an infinite canonical family and, more importantly, a discrete arithmetic set of parameter angles where that ceiling is exactly attained. The mechanism is structural rather than a table lookup: quarter-turn vertices are rotated by the coefficient angle onto the facet-normal lattice. This supplies exact non-Hilbert calibration points for future parameter-profile work without claiming a full profile.
risks: The finding identifies sharp resonance points rather than the complete parameter profile.
